blocks.text: On 27 March 1926, the New Zealand Permanent Air Force photographed the Waimakariri River in what Te Ara identifies as the country’s first aerial survey. Aerial photographs became useful for mapping when flights covered planned lines and frames overlapped, linking image after image across a landscape. By 1930, Lands and Survey was testing photographs for contoured topographic work.

blocks.text: Henry Piet Drury van Asch founded New Zealand Aerial Mapping Ltd in late 1935. The company’s survey work began in 1937, combining aircraft, cameras, pilots, photographers and photogrammetrists to supply imagery and mapping for public and private projects.

blocks.text: The resulting film archive outlasted the aircraft and map editions. LINZ describes nearly 700,000 negatives from about 7,300 surveys flown between 1936 and 2008, including material from New Zealand Aerial Mapping. Negatives, rolls, frame numbers, flight diagrams and indexes were the archive’s working structure; scanning and Retrolens added a new way to search it.

blocks.text: Overlapping photographs could be viewed through a stereoplotter as a three-dimensional model. Ground control anchored that model to known positions and heights; an operator then traced roads, streams, ridges and contours. Analogue instruments such as the Wild A8 made this measurement possible, but the operator still interpreted the terrain.

blocks.text: Aerial mapping ran as a production chain: flights collected images, surveyors established control, photogrammetrists measured features, draughtspeople compiled sheets, and archive staff indexed the negatives. Chapters 3 and 20 follow the move from this film-based workflow to computer-assisted photogrammetry and digital imagery.
